PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 82 — Lesson 106: Osteoporosis & Fracture Prevention

FNP-level goal: Identify people at meaningful fracture risk, distinguish screening from diagnostic evaluation after fragility fracture, interpret DXA and fracture-risk tools in clinical context, look for secondary causes, and coordinate medication, fall prevention, dental, renal, and specialist safety.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain bone remodeling and how aging, menopause, medications, chronic disease, nutrition, falls, and immobility contribute to osteoporosis and fragility fracture.
  • Differentiate osteoporosis screening, diagnosis, fracture-risk estimation, and urgent evaluation of possible acute fracture.
  • Interpret T-scores, Z-scores, and fracture-risk tools as inputs to a patient-specific decision rather than independent diagnoses.
  • Perform a targeted fracture and fall-risk assessment, including medication review, secondary-cause clues, height loss, vertebral symptoms, and functional status.
  • Apply longitudinal prevention, treatment-monitoring, referral, and urgency boundaries for pharmacotherapy, renal disease, hypocalcemia risk, dental issues, and new severe pain.

Part 1 — Osteoporosis Is Silent Until It Is Not

Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone strength and increased fracture susceptibility. Bone strength reflects density and quality. Bone is metabolically active: osteoclast-mediated resorption and osteoblast-mediated formation normally remain balanced. With aging, estrogen deficiency, low body weight, inactivity, smoking, alcohol exposure, nutritional deficits, endocrine disease, chronic inflammation, kidney or liver disease, and some medications, resorption can exceed formation and microarchitecture weakens.

A fragility fracture is often the first visible signal. Hip, vertebral, wrist, humerus, and pelvic fractures can lead to pain, loss of independence, hospitalization, disability, and future fracture risk. The FNP should treat a low-trauma fracture as a diagnostic and prevention opportunity, not as an isolated orthopedic event.

Part 2 — Screening Is Not the Same as Post-Fracture Evaluation

Screening recommendations apply to people without known osteoporosis or fragility fracture. In the United States, current preventive guidance supports DXA screening for women age 65 and older and for younger postmenopausal women at increased risk after clinical risk assessment. Evidence for routine population screening in men is less certain, but clinical judgment and risk-based evaluation remain essential. Patients with prior fragility fracture, secondary causes, or high-risk medications need an individualized diagnostic pathway rather than a screening-only mindset.

Do not wait for a low DXA result to take a fragility fracture seriously. A low-energy hip or vertebral fracture may establish a high-risk state even when a DXA measurement is not severely low. Confirm trauma mechanism, site, prior fractures, fall circumstances, and current functional safety, and coordinate treatment promptly.

Part 3 — DXA, T-Scores, and Z-Scores

DXA commonly measures bone mineral density at the hip and lumbar spine. A T-score compares a patient's density with a young-adult reference population and is used primarily in postmenopausal women and men age 50 and older in the appropriate clinical context. A Z-score compares with age-matched peers and may help signal that secondary causes deserve consideration in younger adults. Numbers must be interpreted alongside age, fracture history, degenerative spinal changes, body size, therapy history, and the quality of the scan.

A DXA result does not measure fall risk, balance, vision, medication burden, or all aspects of bone quality. Conversely, a patient with osteopenia by T-score may have high absolute fracture risk because of age, glucocorticoid exposure, prior fracture, or falls. Use a validated fracture-risk calculation where appropriate, but do not treat a calculator as a substitute for clinical judgment.

Part 4 — The FNP Fracture-Risk Assessment

Ask about prior adult fractures, height loss, kyphosis, back pain, falls, fear of falling, mobility aids, vision, hearing, orthostasis, neuropathy, footwear, home hazards, alcohol, tobacco, dietary intake, physical activity, menopause or hypogonadism context, family history of hip fracture, rheumatoid arthritis, celiac or malabsorption symptoms, thyroid disease, kidney and liver disease, and cancer treatment. Review medications: systemic glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, androgen-deprivation therapy, certain antiseizure medications, proton-pump inhibitors, sedatives, antihypertensives causing orthostasis, and drugs affecting balance all deserve context-specific review.

Measure height over time when feasible, weight, gait, sit-to-stand or balance where safe, posture, vertebral tenderness, and signs of endocrine or nutritional disease. A new acute focal back pain after a minor lift or fall in an older or high-risk patient may be vertebral compression fracture rather than ordinary muscular pain.

Part 5 — Secondary Causes and Laboratory Thinking

Osteoporosis may be primary or secondary. The history and examination guide laboratory and specialty evaluation. Depending on the patient, consider calcium, renal function, liver function, vitamin D status, thyroid testing, blood count, markers of malabsorption, testosterone or reproductive hormone context, parathyroid disease, multiple myeloma concerns, and medication effects. Do not order every test for every patient; ask what explanation is plausible and what result would change management.

Before antiresorptive or anabolic therapy, identify contraindications, renal constraints, hypocalcemia, vitamin D deficiency risk, pregnancy potential, prior radiation or cancer context when relevant, dental history, swallowing or esophageal disease for some oral medications, and the ability to adhere to administration requirements. Treatment choice should be matched to fracture risk, comorbidities, access, and patient priorities.

Part 6 — Fall Prevention Is Bone Treatment

Many fractures occur because fragile bone meets a fall. Review sedating medications, alcohol, orthostatic symptoms, blood pressure treatment, vision correction, footwear, home lighting, throw rugs, stair safety, strength, balance, assistive devices, and emergency-response plans. Refer to physical therapy for strength, balance, gait, and device assessment when appropriate. Treating bone density without reducing falls leaves a major risk pathway untouched.

Weight-bearing and resistance exercise can support bone and function when safe, but recommendations must account for fracture risk, vertebral disease, balance, cardiopulmonary capacity, and pain. Avoid a generic instruction to exercise harder in someone with unstable gait or recent fracture; build a safe, progressive plan.

Part 7 — Medication Treatment and Monitoring Boundaries

Bisphosphonates, denosumab, anabolic therapies, and other agents have different indications, administration, renal considerations, hypocalcemia risks, discontinuation implications, rare adverse effects, and monitoring requirements. An FNP should understand the logic and safety check, but therapy selection and sequencing may require endocrinology, rheumatology, or osteoporosis-specialist collaboration in very high-risk, complex, recurrent-fracture, severe kidney disease, or medication-intolerance situations.

Do not treat medications as interchangeable or stop them abruptly because an injection is inconvenient. For some therapies, missed or stopped doses can have important rebound implications. Build an explicit plan for medication start, calcium and vitamin D adequacy as individualized, dental and jaw symptom counseling, renal or calcium monitoring where relevant, repeat DXA timing, and a reassessment date. Medication holidays, transitions, and duration decisions are individualized rather than automatic.

Part 8 — Urgent Fracture and Neurologic Safety

After a fall, assess pain, ability to bear weight, deformity, neurologic status, anticoagulant use, head injury, and social safety. Hip or pelvic pain with inability to bear weight, deformity, new neurologic deficit, severe uncontrolled pain, or concern for spinal cord compromise requires urgent or emergency evaluation. New severe midline back pain with weakness, bowel or bladder symptoms, fever, cancer history, or trauma needs a separate urgent spine pathway.

A vertebral compression fracture can be subtle. New height loss, kyphosis, acute thoracic or lumbar pain after minimal stress, or pain limiting breathing or mobility should prompt focused evaluation. Do not assume back pain is benign because a patient already has osteoporosis or a previous compression fracture.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Wrist Fracture That Changes the Problem List

A 67-year-old sustains a distal radius fracture after falling from standing height. The FNP reviews the fall, obtains the orthopedic record, assesses prior fracture and medication history, orders or coordinates bone-risk evaluation, screens fall risk, and establishes a prevention plan. The goal is not only healing the wrist; it is preventing the next, potentially hip, fracture.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Low T-Score Is Not the Whole Story

A 60-year-old postmenopausal patient has osteopenia by DXA but chronic prednisone exposure, a prior vertebral fracture, and recurrent falls. The FNP recognizes that fracture risk may be high despite a non-osteoporotic T-score, evaluates secondary contributors, and coordinates treatment planning. Risk is absolute and contextual, not only a threshold on a report.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The New Back Pain

An 80-year-old with osteoporosis develops sudden mid-back pain after lifting a light bag. The FNP assesses focal tenderness, neurologic symptoms, functional decline, and red flags, arranges appropriate imaging or urgent evaluation, controls pain safely, and plans follow-up. A low-energy compression fracture is possible and should not be reduced to a routine muscle strain.

FNP High-Yield Framework: BONE

  1. B — Break history: prior low-trauma fracture, height loss, vertebral symptoms, falls, and function.
  2. O — Obtain the right data: risk-based DXA, fracture-risk assessment, and targeted secondary-cause evaluation.
  3. N — Notice fall and medication risk: vision, gait, home safety, sedatives, orthostasis, steroids, and access barriers.
  4. E — Establish longitudinal safety: individualized therapy, calcium and vitamin D context, renal and dental considerations, monitoring, and specialty referral.

Take-Home Summary

Osteoporosis prevention is fracture prevention. Use screening guidance in the appropriate population, but recognize that a fragility fracture or high-risk medication changes the clinical question. DXA and risk tools inform decisions; they do not replace fall assessment, secondary-cause evaluation, medication safety, or specialist collaboration. The FNP protects independence by treating both bone fragility and fall risk.

Educational note: This lesson supports FNP clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized fracture-risk assessment, DXA interpretation, medication labeling, dental or renal consultation, or specialist care. New inability to bear weight, severe pain after a fall, deformity, head injury on anticoagulation, progressive neurologic deficit, or suspected spinal emergency requires urgent or emergency evaluation.
